name: Mitochondrial Complex I Deficiency (NADH:Ubiquinone Oxidoreductase Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: Complex I deficiency is the single most common defect of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and the commonest biochemical cause of Leigh syndrome.

Complex I is the largest respiratory chain enzyme, built from dozens of subunits; seven core subunits are encoded by mitochondrial DNA (the MT-ND genes) and the remainder plus assembly factors are nuclear-encoded, so inheritance may be autosomal recessive, maternal or (rarely) X-linked.

Nuclear structural or assembly-factor defects (e.g. NDUFS1, NDUFS4, NDUFS7, NDUFS8, NDUFV1, NDUFA1, NDUFAF1-8, ACAD9, FOXRED1, NUBPL) typically present in the neonatal period or infancy with encephalopathy, hypotonia and lactic acidosis.

The distinctive mtDNA-related phenotypes arise almost exclusively at Complex I: MT-ND point variants underlie the majority of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, and ND-gene variants are a recognised cause of MELAS and of maternally inherited Leigh syndrome.
ACAD9 deficiency is a treatable Complex I assembly disorder in which riboflavin supplementation may improve the exercise-intolerant cardiomyopathy/myopathy phenotype, so it should be actively sought.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, leukoencephalopathy with characteristic cavitating white-matter change, and Leigh-type brainstem/basal ganglia signal abnormality are recurring imaging and organ patterns.
Raised lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid with an elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio suggests a respiratory chain lesion, but normal lactate does not exclude Complex I deficiency.

Isolated Complex I deficiency on muscle or fibroblast respiratory chain enzymology, with normal activity of the other complexes, narrows the genetic search to Complex I structural, assembly and MT-ND genes.
reference.pathophysiology: Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is the entry point of the electron transport chain, oxidising NADH generated by the Krebs cycle and beta-oxidation, transferring electrons via flavin mononucleotide and a chain of iron-sulphur clusters to ubiquinone, and pumping protons to build the transmembrane electrochemical gradient that powers ATP synthesis. It is the largest of the oxidative phosphorylation enzymes, an L-shaped assembly of a membrane arm and a peripheral matrix arm comprising many subunits; seven hydrophobic core subunits (ND1-ND6 and ND4L) are encoded by mitochondrial DNA (the MT-ND genes) while the remaining structural subunits and a large set of dedicated assembly factors are nuclear-encoded. Pathogenic variants in nuclear genes such as NDUFS1, NDUFS4, NDUFS7, NDUFS8, NDUFV1, NDUFA1 (X-linked), the assembly factors NDUFAF1-NDUFAF8, ACAD9, FOXRED1 and NUBPL, or maternally transmitted MT-ND variants, destabilise the holoenzyme or impair its assembly, causing loss of NADH oxidation, a bottleneck in electron flow, secondary lactic acidosis from redirected pyruvate, and energy failure that most severely affects high-demand tissues such as brain, heart and skeletal muscle.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial Complex III deficiency (ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase defect, including BCS1L/GRACILE)
Mitochondrial Complex IV deficiency (cytochrome c oxidase / COX defect, e.g. SURF1 Leigh syndrome)
Mitochondrial Complex V deficiency (ATP synthase defect, e.g. TMEM70, MT-ATP6 NARP/MILS)
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiencies from mtDNA depletion or maintenance defects and mitochondrial translation defects
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency and other primary lactic acidoses
Biotinidase deficiency and other treatable causes of Leigh-like brainstem encephalopathy
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy from other causes and dominant optic atrophy for the isolated optic phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate with lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Plasma amino acids (alanine) and urine organic acids
Spectrophotometric respiratory chain enzyme activities in skeletal muscle or cultured fibroblasts showing isolated Complex I reduction
Neuroimaging (magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy) for symmetrical basal ganglia/brainstem lesions and a lactate peak
Molecular genetic testing including a mitochondrial nuclear gene panel or exome plus whole mitochondrial genome sequencing
Echocardiography and electrocardiography to detect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and conduction disease
Blue-native gel electrophoresis and immunodetection of Complex I assembly in tissue or fibroblasts
redFlags: Rapidly progressive brainstem dysfunction with respiratory irregularity, apnoea or swallowing failure in an encephalopathic infant
Decompensated lactic acidosis with cardiorespiratory instability during intercurrent illness or fasting
New or worsening hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with heart failure or arrhythmia
Acute stroke-like episodes with seizures suggesting a MELAS-type presentation
Sudden bilateral painless visual loss suggesting Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is heterogeneous and gene- and phenotype-dependent: severe neonatal and Leigh-type presentations often progress to early death, whereas some later-onset myopathic, optic or riboflavin-responsive ACAD9 phenotypes are more indolent. Overall the disorder is chronic and frequently life-limiting, with course punctuated by metabolic decompensation during catabolic stress.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal blood lactate excludes the diagnosis, when cerebrospinal fluid lactate or an elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio may be the only clue.
Overlooking the treatable riboflavin-responsive ACAD9-related Complex I deficiency and other cofactor-responsive forms.
Attributing an isolated optic or stroke-like presentation to a non-mitochondrial cause and missing an MT-ND variant.
Failing to appreciate that maternal, autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance all occur, which misdirects counselling if only one mode is considered.
Using sodium valproate or other mitochondrial toxins, or unbuffered fasting/anaesthesia, which can precipitate decompensation.
references: Textbook of inherited metabolic disease (mitochondrial disorders chapter)
Neurology reference on mitochondrial and respiratory chain disease
International consensus guidance on diagnosis and management of mitochondrial disease
management: No curative therapy; supportive treatment uses a mitochondrial cofactor regimen of riboflavin, coenzyme Q10 and antioxidants, and a riboflavin trial should be actively pursued in ACAD9-related disease as this subtype can be riboflavin-responsive
Consider idebenone for the Leber hereditary optic neuropathy phenotype caused by MT-ND variants
Treat acute metabolic decompensation and lactic acidosis promptly with intravenous dextrose and fluids, and avoid prolonged fasting and catabolic stress
Avoid mitochondrial toxins such as sodium valproate and aminoglycosides that can precipitate deterioration
Symptomatic control of seizures, dystonia and spasticity, with anticonvulsant choice mindful of hepatotoxicity
Surveillance for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and conduction disease with echocardiography and ECG, alongside monitoring of neurological, feeding and respiratory status
Multidisciplinary care and genetic counselling reflecting the relevant autosomal recessive, maternal or X-linked inheritance, with prenatal and reproductive options
